name: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) cervical lordosis

lead: CBP is a chiropractic system that tries to restore the neck's forward curve (cervical lordosis) using traction, exercises and adjustments.
Most supporting studies come from CBP-affiliated authors, and critics question whether curve changes relate to symptoms.

paras: Practitioners measure curves on X-rays and apply sustained extension traction, orthotics and Mirror Image positioning intended to produce lasting tissue change.
Repeated X-rays add radiation exposure, and neck manipulation has been associated with rare stroke. Certification is voluntary.

lead: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) is a posture-focused chiropractic technique founded in 1980 by Donald Harrison, Deanne Harrison and Daniel Murphy. It uses mathematical models of ideal spinal curves, and combines adjustments, exercises and traction to try to restore them [1]. Cervical lordosis, the natural forward curve of the neck, is one of its main targets.

Proponents claim that restoring the curve reduces pain and improves posture. Grokipedia, which draws mainly on CBP-affiliated sources, describes a body of mostly CBP-authored studies, while noting critics who question whether curve deviations relate to symptoms and point to weak study designs [1].
infobox: Donald D. Harrison, Deanne Harrison, Daniel Murphy
Mirror Image adjustments, exercises, extension traction, Denneroll orthotic

paras: CBP uses a Harrison Spinal Model that describes the cervical curve as a circular arc and defines target angles [1]. Its signature approach, called Mirror Image, positions the patient opposite to their abnormal posture [1]. Sustained extension traction, typically 10 to 20 minutes per session, and foam orthotics such as the Denneroll are used in clinic and at home [1]. Cervical traction protocols were refined by Deed Harrison between 1996 and 2000 [1].

According to Grokipedia, a lateral X-ray study reported mean cervical angles of about 34.5 degrees in asymptomatic people, 28.6 in acute neck pain and 22.0 in chronic neck pain [1]. A non-randomized trial of CBP extension-compression traction plus manipulation reported a 13.6 degree gain in C2-C7 Cobb angle and reduced pain, with about 70 percent of participants retaining gains at 14 months while controls showed no change [1]. The same source cites roughly 21 randomized trials among CBP-affiliated publications [1].

Critics noted in that source observe that sagittal curve deviations occur in many people without symptoms, that many trials are non-randomized with mixed treatments, and that most sources are CBP-affiliated [1]. No independent systematic review was loaded for this article.

A rapid review cited by Grokipedia found no good evidence that routine spinal X-rays improve outcomes, raising radiation exposure questions, since CBP uses radiographs to measure curves [1]. Chiropractic neck manipulation in general has been linked to rare vertebral artery stroke, with disputed causality [2].
